hints: Start from what you actually measured in the burette. Work out moles of thiosulfate using $n = c \times V$ with volume in $\text{dm}^3$.
Use the two given equations to link moles of thiosulfate back to moles of $\text{I}_2$ and then to moles of $\text{ClO}^-$ in the $25.0 \text{ cm}^3$ portion.
Remember the $25.0 \text{ cm}^3$ portion is only one tenth of the $250 \text{ cm}^3$ flask, which itself came from only $10.0 \text{ cm}^3$ of original bleach.
walkthrough:
Find moles of thiosulfate actually used**
You titrated the liberated iodine with thiosulfate, so that is your starting point. Convert $20.80 \text{ cm}^3$ to $\text{dm}^3$ by dividing by 1000. $$n(\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}) = 0.100 \times \frac{20.80}{1000} = 2.08 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$

Work backwards through the two equations**
Look at the second equation: $\text{I}_2 + 2\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-} \rightarrow 2\text{I}^- + \text{S}_4\text{O}_6^{2-}$. Two moles of thiosulfate react with one mole of $\text{I}_2$. Then the first equation shows one mole of $\text{ClO}^-$ makes one mole of $\text{I}_2$. So moles of $\text{ClO}^-$ in the $25.0 \text{ cm}^3$ aliquot is half the thiosulfate moles: $$n(\text{ClO}^-) = \frac{2.08 \times 10^{-3}}{2} = 1.04 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$

Scale up for dilution then back to original bleach**
That $1.04 \times 10^{-3}$ mol was only in $25.0 \text{ cm}^3$. The flask holds $250 \text{ cm}^3$, ten times more, so multiply by 10: $1.04 \times 10^{-2}$ mol. All of that came from the original $10.0 \text{ cm}^3$ of bleach. Divide by its volume in $\text{dm}^3$: $$c = \frac{1.04 \times 10^{-2}}{10.0/1000} = 1.04 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$

Final answer: moles $\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-} = 0.100 \times 20.80/1000 = 2.08 \times 10^{-3}$
moles $\text{ClO}^-$ in $25.0 \text{ cm}^3 = 2.08 \times 10^{-3}/2 = 1.04 \times 10^{-3}$, so in $250 \text{ cm}^3 = 1.04 \times 10^{-2}$
concentration of $\text{ClO}^- = 1.04 \times 10^{-2}/(10.0/1000) = 1.04 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$

hints: Think which indicator forms a deep blue complex specifically with iodine.
walkthrough:
Recall the iodine test**
Whenever iodine is present in a titration, starch is the classic choice because it forms an intense blue-black complex with $\text{I}_2$, making the end-point very sharp.

hints: Picture the starch-iodine complex at the start and what remains when all the iodine has been converted to colourless iodide.
walkthrough:
Visualise the disappearance of iodine**
Before the end-point free $\text{I}_2$ with starch gives a deep blue or black colour. At the end-point all $\text{I}_2$ has been reduced to $\text{I}^-$, which is colourless, so the blue colour just vanishes.
Final answer: blue or black to colourless

hints: Consider why adding starch when iodine concentration is still very high can trap iodine and blur the end-point.
walkthrough:
Protect the sharpness of the end-point**
If you add starch too early, a large amount of iodine binds strongly to starch and is slow to react, giving a smeared end-point. So you titrate first until the brown iodine colour fades to pale yellow, then add starch to see the final blue to colourless change clearly.
Final answer: towards or close to the end-point of the titration, when the solution goes pale yellow

hints: Convert the measured oxygen volume to moles using the room temperature molar volume, $24000 \text{ cm}^3 \text{ mol}^{-1}$.

Use the equation $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2 + \text{NaClO} \rightarrow \text{NaCl} + \text{O}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$ to link moles of $\text{O}_2$ to moles of $\text{ClO}^-$ and divide by the $5.0 \text{ cm}^3$ sample volume.
walkthrough:
Turn gas volume into moles**
At room temperature and pressure one mole of gas occupies $24000 \text{ cm}^3$. So: $$n(\text{O}_2) = \frac{82}{24000} = 3.42 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$ The equation shows a 1:1 ratio, $1 \text{ O}_2$ from $1 \text{ ClO}^-$, so this is also moles of $\text{ClO}^-$ in the $5.0 \text{ cm}^3$ sample.

Convert to concentration**
Divide by the bleach volume in $\text{dm}^3$: $$c(\text{ClO}^-) = \frac{3.42 \times 10^{-3}}{5.0/1000} = 0.68 \text{ to } 0.684 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$

Final answer: moles $\text{O}_2 = 82/24000 = 3.42 \times 10^{-3} =$ moles $\text{ClO}^-$
concentration of $\text{ClO}^- = 3.42 \times 10^{-3}/(5.0/1000) = 0.683 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$

hints: Write products over reactants with each concentration raised to the power of its balancing number in the equation.
walkthrough:
Apply the Kc rule directly**
For $\text{C}_3\text{Cl}_3\text{N}_3\text{O}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{C}_3\text{H}_3\text{N}_3\text{O}_3 + 3\text{HClO}$, put product concentrations on top and reactant concentrations below, each raised to its coefficient: $$K_c = \frac{[\text{C}_3\text{H}_3\text{N}_3\text{O}_3][\text{HClO}]^3}{[\text{C}_3\text{Cl}_3\text{N}_3\text{O}_3][\text{H}_2\text{O}]^3}$$

hints: Identify which species in the (d) equilibrium is being removed by sunlight and predict which way the system must shift to replace it.
Recall which factors change $K_c$ and whether a concentration change at constant temperature is one of them.
walkthrough:
Use Le Chatelier thinking**
Sunlight decomposes $\text{HClO}$, so $[\text{HClO}]$ falls. The system opposes this loss by favouring the forward reaction to make more $\text{HClO}$. That means the position of equilibrium shifts to the right.

Separate position from constant**
$K_c$ depends only on temperature. Removing a product or shifting position does not change its value at constant temperature, so $K_c$ is unchanged.

Final answer: position of equilibrium moves to the right, forward reaction predominates to make more $\text{HClO}$ as $[\text{HClO}]$ decreases
no effect on $K_c$

hints: The gas that relights a glowing splint is oxygen, so write a decomposition of $\text{HClO}$ that produces $\text{O}_2$ with chloride as the other product.
walkthrough:
Build the redox decomposition**
A glowing splint relighting tells you $\text{O}_2$ is formed. Chlorine in $\text{HClO}$ is +1 and is reduced to -1 in $\text{HCl}$, while oxygen is oxidised to $\text{O}_2$. Balancing gives: $$2\text{HClO} \rightarrow 2\text{HCl} + \text{O}_2$$

hints: For added acid, think which base component of the $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$/$\text{HCO}_3^-$ pair can mop up $\text{H}^+$.
For added alkali, think which acid component reacts with $\text{OH}^-$ to keep $[\text{H}^+]$ almost constant.
walkthrough:
See how added acid is removed**
The buffer contains a large reserve of $\text{HCO}_3^-$ which acts as a base. Added $\text{H}^+$ is consumed: $$\text{H}^+ + \text{HCO}_3^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$$ This prevents $[\text{H}^+]$ rising much, so pH stays almost constant.

See how added alkali is removed**
The buffer contains a large reserve of $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$ which acts as an acid. Added $\text{OH}^-$ is neutralised: $$\text{OH}^- + \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightarrow \text{HCO}_3^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Again $[\text{H}^+]$ and pH barely change because the ratio $[\text{HCO}_3^-]/[\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3]$ hardly shifts.

Final answer: addition of acid: $\text{H}^+ + \text{HCO}_3^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$ or $\text{H}^+ + \text{HCO}_3^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2$
addition of base: $\text{OH}^- + \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightarrow \text{HCO}_3^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$

hints: Rearrange $K_a = [\text{H}^+][\text{HCO}_3^-]/[\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3]$ to make $[\text{H}^+]$ the subject using the given ratio 9.5:1.
Take $-\log$ of your $[\text{H}^+]$ value to get pH.
walkthrough:
Calculate hydrogen ion concentration from Ka**
From $K_a = \frac{[\text{H}^+][\text{HCO}_3^-]}{[\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3]}$, rearrange: $$[\text{H}^+] = K_a \times \frac{[\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3]}{[\text{HCO}_3^-]} = 7.94 \times 10^{-7} \times \frac{1}{9.5} = 8.36 \times 10^{-8} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$

Convert to pH**
$$\text{pH} = -\log(8.36 \times 10^{-8}) = 7.08$$ This slightly acidic shift from 7.40 fits a lower $\text{HCO}_3^-$ to $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$ ratio.

Final answer: $[\text{H}^+] = (7.94 \times 10^{-7}) \times 1/9.5 = 8.36 \times 10^{-8}$
$\text{pH} = -\log[\text{H}^+] = 7.08$
